brief: Prepare a one-page experiment brief for After Hours, a fictional £35 London club night. Record the user's visual prediction, the approved readout of the first run, the chosen follow-up, and selected guardrails. Use only approved decisions and label open questions. The data is simulated and the first run was observational. This task authorizes drafting only.

cards.question: Which page sells more tickets?
cards.context: One London club night. Two £35 ticket pages. Make your call before opening the sales report.

options.label: A · The poster
options.detail: A full-bleed crowd photograph and a headline that takes over the page. The ticket price sits beside the final call to action.

options.label: B · The box office
options.detail: A compact photograph, prominent price and ticket details, followed by a solid purchase button.

cards.reason: The crowd sells the feeling of being there. That is a design hunch.
cards.action: Record the selected design as my prediction in the brief.
cards.source: Two original mockups for the same fictional show, venue, price and purchase offer. The concert photograph was generated for this example.
cards.uncertainty: These visuals alone cannot establish which design converts better.

cards.question: Would you send this headline?
cards.context: The first sales report is in. Each page received 10,000 eligible visits. A recorded 520 paid orders (5.2%) and B recorded 380 (3.8%).
cards.before: The poster design increased ticket sales by 37%.
cards.after: The poster page recorded 140 more orders. We still need to check who saw each page.
cards.reason: The 140-order lead is observable. The two pages may have reached different audiences.
cards.action: Use the approved wording in the experiment brief.
cards.source: Simulated seven-day ticket-shop log. A had 520 orders from 10,000 visits. B had 380 from 10,000. The relative difference is 36.8%, rounded to 37% in the proposed headline.
cards.uncertainty: Page assignment followed campaign traffic and was not randomized. An order counts once per eligible visit.

cards.question: Which design earns a rematch?
cards.context: B leads on both devices. Mobile was 40/2,000 (2%) for A and 240/8,000 (3%) for B. Desktop was 480/8,000 (6%) for A and 140/2,000 (7%) for B. A got four times as many desktop visits.

options.label: B · Test the box office
options.detail: Make B the challenger against A in a device-balanced test.

options.label: A · Back the poster
options.detail: Keep A as the preferred design and challenge that choice against B.

options.label: Hold both designs
options.detail: Audit campaign and checkout instrumentation before scheduling a test.

cards.reason: With the same 50/50 device mix, A models at 4% and B at 5%. The extra percentage point is a hypothesis worth testing.
cards.action: Draft the selected next step for the promoter.
cards.source: Simulated counts by device. Equal weighting gives A = (2% + 6%)/2 = 4% and B = (3% + 7%)/2 = 5%. This is standardization to an illustrative audience mix.
cards.uncertainty: Adjusting for device does not remove campaign, time, or audience differences. A controlled test is needed for a causal claim.

cards.question: What would make you stop the test?
cards.context: For a rematch, randomly split traffic 1:1 within each device type and track paid orders per eligible visit. Choose the warning signs to monitor. If you chose to hold, these become checks for the audit.

options.label: Payment errors
options.detail: Flag a rise of 0.5 percentage points in failed payments per checkout attempt versus control.

options.label: Mobile load time
options.detail: Flag a 0.3-second regression in mobile p75 Largest Contentful Paint versus control.

options.label: Refund requests
options.detail: Flag a rise of 1 percentage point in seven-day refund requests per order versus control.

cards.recommendation: Watch payment errors and mobile speed.
cards.reason: The two checks catch a broken checkout or a slower page while the test is running.
cards.action: Add the selected monitoring thresholds to the brief for review.
cards.source: Illustrative operating thresholds proposed for this fictional test. A threshold crossing triggers an investigation and a decision about pausing.
cards.uncertainty: Baseline variation, sample size and duration need sizing with real traffic before launch.
